sections.h: Wisdom of Solomon 13: from the works to the Maker
sections.b: The fullest argument for knowing God from creation in the Greek Old Testament is Wisdom of Solomon 13:1–9. People saw fire, wind, stars and water and took them for gods; they should have reasoned that the Source of their beauty and power is greater still, for "their Maker is seen, by analogy" (Wisdom of Solomon 13:5). They deserve "small" blame, since they were seeking God, but they "are not to be excused" (Wisdom of Solomon 13:6–8). Paul's argument in Romans 1:19–25 follows the same steps. The word "by analogy" (analogōs) later gave its name to the Christian debate about how far creatures resemble God: the Catechism cites the verse (Catechism 41), John of Damascus opens his Exact Exposition with it, and Karl Barth rejected the "analogy of being" outright.

common: Wisdom of Solomon 13:1–9 is widely held to stand behind Paul's argument in Romans 1:18–32.
uncommon: Some readers stress that Wisdom of Solomon is gentler than Paul: it says nature-worshipers were seeking God and deserve little blame (Wisdom of Solomon 13:6).

sections.h: Wisdom of Solomon 13–15: the satire on idols
sections.b: Wisdom of Solomon 13:10–15:19 is the longest attack on idols in the Greek Old Testament. It retells Isaiah 44: a woodcutter makes a god from the knotty scrap left after his cooking fire, nails it to the wall so it will not fall, and prays to it for health, life and success (Wisdom of Solomon 13:11–19). It explains how idolatry began, from a grieving father's image of his dead child and from the images of distant kings (Wisdom of Solomon 14:15–20), and it traces every evil to it: "Worship of idols too vile to name / is the start of every evil, its cause and its end" (Wisdom of Solomon 14:27). A potter makes a god from the same clay as his pots (Wisdom of Solomon 15:7–13), a passage that Romans 9:21 seems to echo. The list of vices in Wisdom of Solomon 14:22–27 is the closest Jewish parallel to Romans 1:29–31.
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 13:10–15:19; Isaiah 44:9–20; Psalm 115:4–8; Romans 1:21–32; Romans 9:21

sections.h: The plagues retold in Wisdom of Solomon
sections.b: Wisdom of Solomon 11–19 retells the plagues as a series of contrasts, built on one rule: "The very things that punished their enemies / were the things that did them good when they were in need" (Wisdom of Solomon 11:5). The Nile turned to blood as a rebuke for Pharaoh's order to drown the babies, while Israel drank from the rock (Wisdom of Solomon 11:6–14). Egypt worshiped animals and was punished by swarms of animals, "so that they would know this: / what a person sins with, he is punished with" (Wisdom of Solomon 11:15–16). The writer adds that God held back and punished "a little at a time", to leave room for repentance (Wisdom of Solomon 12:2; Wisdom of Solomon 12:10).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 11:5–16; Wisdom of Solomon 12:23–27; Exodus 7:20–21; Exodus 8:2–6; Exodus 17:6

sections.h: Formless matter, and measure, number and weight
sections.b: Wisdom of Solomon says God's hand "created the world out of formless matter" (Wisdom of Solomon 11:17), a phrase from Greek philosophy that may mean the shapeless earth of Genesis 1:2 or matter that existed before the world. Readers set it beside 2 Maccabees 7:28, where God made the world "not from things that were", and the churches' answers are on the card at 2 Maccabees 7. The same chapter says God set everything "by measure, by number and by weight" (Wisdom of Solomon 11:20), a line Augustine quotes in The City of God (11.30) and that medieval writers used for the order of creation. God loves all he made: "nothing you made disgusts you, / for if you had hated a thing you would never have fashioned it" (Wisdom of Solomon 11:24).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 11:17; Wisdom of Solomon 11:20; Wisdom of Solomon 11:24; Genesis 1:2; 2 Maccabees 7:28

sections.h: Mercy because of power (Wisdom of Solomon 11–12)
sections.b: Wisdom of Solomon makes God's power the reason for his mercy: "Yet because you can do all things, you show mercy to all" (Wisdom of Solomon 11:23). Before God the world is like a speck on a scale or a drop of dew (Wisdom of Solomon 11:22, from Isaiah 40:15). He spares all because they are his, "Master, lover of souls" (Wisdom of Solomon 11:26), and he was patient even with the Canaanites (Wisdom of Solomon 12:8–10). The lesson for his people: "whoever is righteous must love people" (Wisdom of Solomon 12:19), and when judged, "we will look for mercy" (Wisdom of Solomon 12:22). Chapter 15 opens with the words of Exodus 34:6: God is kind and true, slow to anger, ruling with mercy (Wisdom of Solomon 15:1).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 11:21–12:2; Wisdom of Solomon 12:19–22; Wisdom of Solomon 15:1; Isaiah 40:15; Exodus 34:6

sections.h: "Room for repentance" in Wisdom of Solomon
sections.b: Wisdom of Solomon says God overlooks sins "to bring them to repentance" (Wisdom of Solomon 11:23), corrects sinners "a little at a time" (Wisdom of Solomon 12:2) and gave even the Canaanites "room for repentance" (Wisdom of Solomon 12:10), the same Greek phrase Hebrews uses of Esau, who "found no place for repentance" (Hebrews 12:17). God grants repentance when people sin, which gives his children hope (Wisdom of Solomon 12:19). Paul uses the same thought: God's kindness "is leading you to repentance" (Romans 2:4).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 11:23; Wisdom of Solomon 12:2; Wisdom of Solomon 12:10; Wisdom of Solomon 12:19; Hebrews 12:17; Romans 2:4

sections.h: Wisdom of Solomon on the conquest of Canaan
sections.b: Wisdom of Solomon 12:3–11 is one of the earliest Jewish reflections on the justice of the conquest. It lists the Canaanites' crimes, sorcery, child sacrifice and cannibal feasts, in terms partly from the Torah (Deuteronomy 18:9–12) and partly from Greek polemic against mystery cults. It insists that God "spared even them, since they were human" (Wisdom of Solomon 12:8), sending wasps to drive them out slowly and giving them room to repent (Wisdom of Solomon 12:8–10), as Exodus says the nations would be driven out bit by bit (Exodus 23:30). It goes beyond the Torah in calling their wickedness inborn and them "a seed cursed from the beginning" (Wisdom of Solomon 12:10–11).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 12:3–11; Deuteronomy 18:9–12; Exodus 23:28–30; Deuteronomy 7:20–22; Genesis 15:16

sections.h: How images of kings became gods (Wisdom of Solomon 14)
sections.b: Wisdom of Solomon 14:16–20 describes the ruler cult from inside: people who lived far from their king made an image of him to flatter him as if he were present; the artist, hoping to please, made the likeness finer than the man; and the crowds, charmed by the art, came to treat as an object of worship the man they had honored shortly before. "Absolute rulers gave orders, and carved images were worshiped" (Wisdom of Solomon 14:16). Written in Egypt, where the Ptolemies were worshiped as gods, the passage stands between Daniel's golden statue (Daniel 3) and Revelation's image of the beast (Revelation 13:14–15).

sections.h: "What a person sins with, he is punished with"
sections.b: Wisdom of Solomon makes fitting punishment the rule of the Exodus: Egypt worshiped animals, so animals plagued it, "so that they would know this: / what a person sins with, he is punished with" (Wisdom of Solomon 11:16). The Nile that drowned Israel's babies turned to blood (Wisdom of Solomon 11:6–7), and the gods the Egyptians trusted became the means of their punishment (Wisdom of Solomon 12:23–27). The rabbis taught the same rule: "With the measure that a person measures, he is measured with it" (Mishnah Sotah 1:7). The writer stresses the purpose: a fitting punishment teaches the sinner what he did.
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 11:5–16; Wisdom of Solomon 12:23–27; Matthew 7:2; Psalm 7:15–16

sections.h: Egypt's animal gods in Wisdom of Solomon
sections.b: Wisdom of Solomon, probably written in Alexandria, attacks the Egyptian worship of animals again and again: "mindless reptiles and worthless vermin" (Wisdom of Solomon 11:15), "the most worthless even of hateful animals" (Wisdom of Solomon 12:24), creatures without beauty that "God's praise and God's blessing have both passed" by (Wisdom of Solomon 15:18–19). Egypt, "the enemies of your people who oppressed them", is the most foolish of all, worshiping every idol and the lowest beasts (Wisdom of Solomon 15:14–15). Philo, in the same city, scorns the Egyptian honor given to bulls, crocodiles, the asp, ibises and hawks (On the Decalogue 76–79).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 11:15; Wisdom of Solomon 12:23–27; Wisdom of Solomon 15:14–19; Exodus 12:12

sections.b: Wisdom of Solomon is one of the first Jewish books to use the Greek philosophers' word pronoia, "providence", for God's care: "But your providence, Father, is at the helm" of every ship, "for you have given a road even in the sea" (Wisdom of Solomon 14:3, echoing Isaiah 43:16). God steered Noah's raft, and so "the world's hope fled for safety onto a raft" (Wisdom of Solomon 14:6). The same word returns in the darkness of Egypt (Wisdom of Solomon 17:2).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 14:3–6; Wisdom of Solomon 17:2; Isaiah 43:16; Matthew 6:26–30

sections.h: The proud giants in Wisdom of Solomon
sections.b: Wisdom of Solomon recalls the Flood as the time "when the proud giants were dying", and the ark as a raft that carried "the world's hope" (Wisdom of Solomon 14:6). It shares the Jewish tradition, found also in Sirach 16:7, Baruch 3:26–28 and 3 Maccabees 2:4, that the giants of Genesis 6:4 were destroyed for their pride, but it says nothing of the fallen angels of 1 Enoch.
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 14:6; Genesis 6:4; Sirach 16:7; Baruch 3:26–28; 3 Maccabees 2:4

sections.h: "The One Who Is" and "the Name that can be shared with no one"
sections.b: Wisdom of Solomon calls God "the One Who Is" (Wisdom of Solomon 13:1), the Septuagint's rendering of God's self-naming in Exodus 3:14, and it says idolaters "gave to stones and wood the Name that can be shared with no one" (Wisdom of Solomon 14:21), the KJV's "incommunicable name". Thomas Aquinas quotes that verse when he argues that the name "God" belongs properly to God alone (Summa Theologiae I, question 13, article 9).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 13:1; Wisdom of Solomon 14:21; Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 42:8

sections.h: Wisdom's last act in Wisdom of Solomon
sections.b: After guiding the righteous from Adam to the Red Sea (Wisdom of Solomon 10), Wisdom acts as a person one last time: she "made their works succeed / through the hand of a holy prophet", Moses (Wisdom of Solomon 11:1). From Wisdom of Solomon 11:4 the speaker addresses God directly, and in the rest of the book God himself acts in the Exodus. Wisdom is still the "craftsman's wisdom" behind ships (Wisdom of Solomon 14:2) and God's wisdom whose works should not lie idle (Wisdom of Solomon 14:5).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 11:1–4; Wisdom of Solomon 14:2; Wisdom of Solomon 14:5; Wisdom of Solomon 10:15–21
